For \(n=2\), \(\varphi(2)=1\). The condition \((*)\) becomes \( (2y)^2+1 \mid x^{\varphi(2)}-1 \), so

Let \(A = y^2+1\) and \(B = 4y^2+1\).
We calculate their greatest common divisor:
\(\gcd(A,B) = \gcd(y^2+1, 4y^2+1)\).

If \(y \equiv 2 \pmod 3\), then \(y^2 \equiv 4 \equiv 1 \pmod 3\), so \(y^2+1 \equiv 2 \pmod 3\).

This means \(\gcd(A,B)=1\).
So, \(\text{lcm}(A,B) = AB = (y^2+1)(4y^2+1)\).

\[ x-1 = C(y^2+1)(4y^2+1) \]

\[
f(x)=\begin{cases}0,&0\le x<1,\\1,&x=1.\end{cases}
\]
Assume that \((f_n)\) converges uniformly. Uniform convergence implies pointwise convergence, so its uniform limit must be \(f\). Set \(\varepsilon=\tfrac14\). For every \(N\in\mathbb Z_+\), choose \(n=N\) and \(x=2^{-1/n}\in[0,1)\). Then \(f(x)=0\), while
\[
|f_n(x)-f(x)|=x^n=\frac12>\varepsilon.
\]
Thus no \(N\) satisfies the uniform-convergence condition.
